This bill is part of a package that would create a new accountability system for banks, insurers and superannuation funds.
The system would apply to banking six months after the bill starts, and to insurance and superannuation 18 months after that start.
New entrants to those industries would be covered from the time they become an ADI or non-operating holding company, or from when they become licensed.
The package would establish a new accountability regime for banking, insurance and superannuation.
It would set different start dates for banking (six months) and insurance and superannuation (18 months) after the bill commences.
New industry entrants would be subject to the regime from the time they become an ADI, non-operating holding company or licensed entity.
Banks, insurers and superannuation funds, including new entrants to those industries.

The Financial Accountability Regime Bill 2022 establishes the Financial Accountability Regime (FAR), replacing the Banking Executive Accountability Regime to extend heightened accountability obligations to banks, insurers, and superannuation entities. The FAR requires at least 40% of variable remuneration for accountable persons to be deferred for a minimum of four years, with reductions for breaches, and gives APRA and ASIC powers to disqualify individuals, investigate breaches, and seek civil penalties, applying to banking six months after royal assent and to insurance and superannuation 18 months after.

The speaker moved to discharge the Financial Accountability Regime Bill 2022 from the Notice Paper and opposed it, arguing that Stephen Jones is protecting bankers by removing penalties, and criticised former Labor premier Anna Bligh as head of the Australian Banking Association.
